title: Information Ecology Mechanics — Attention, Repetition, Memory, Correction and Forgetting
purpose: Describe how information survives, spreads, mutates, concentrates, disappears and becomes collective memory across people, platforms, institutions and archives.
unit_of_analysis: A claim/object plus its copies, framings, audiences, corrections, sources and memory traces.
flow_model: source → encoding → channel → exposure → interpretation → repetition/remix → archive → retrieval → correction/revision → memory or forgetting

quantities.meaning: How many opportunities existed for an audience to encounter the object/claim?
quantities.caution: Usually platform-specific and not equivalent to unique people.

quantities.meaning: How many people or institutions repeat, endorse, act on or incorporate it?
quantities.caution: Repetition can be criticism rather than endorsement.

quantities.meaning: How many apparently separate repetitions come from genuinely independent provenance roots?
How much origin, sequence, date and qualification survive through recirculation?
How far corrective material travels relative to the original claim?
How likely a future searcher is to find the object and its provenance/correction.
The time over which attention or retrieval decays in a defined environment.
quantities.caution: Empirical fit required; not assumed to be exponential.

quantities.meaning: How dependent durable memory is on a few platforms, archives or institutions.

mechanisms.description: Many visible sources repeat one root source, creating an illusion of independent confirmation.
mechanisms.test: Cluster citations/links/textual lineage before counting sources.

mechanisms.description: Repeated exposure can make a claim feel familiar regardless of truth.
Quotes, clips and summaries may retain the memorable fragment while losing timing, trigger, scope or uncertainty.
mechanisms.test: Compare each derivative object with the nearest recoverable source context.

mechanisms.description: A correction may reach fewer people or travel through different channels than the original.
mechanisms.test: Measure audience overlap and linkage where possible.

mechanisms.description: Searchable archives can stabilize an old representation long after the underlying status changes.
mechanisms.test: Check whether later corrections, dismissals or revisions are linked and comparably discoverable.

mechanisms.description: Conflict, novelty or target production can become a repeatable source of content/status/revenue.
mechanisms.test: Trace incentives and outputs; do not infer motive solely from high engagement.

mechanisms.description: Material can disappear through deletion, link rot, platform closure, inaccessible formats or loss of social relevance.
Provenance restoration, contextual annotation and correction linkage can improve future interpretation without deleting history.
mechanisms.test: Preserve original state plus dated repair.

ecology_states.description: Multiple sources and interpretations remain visible, correction is possible, provenance is recoverable.
Information is distributed across incompatible archives or communities with weak common context.
One interpretation/source dominates retrieval despite possible alternatives.
High repetition, low provenance clarity, role lock, conflict incentives and weak correction combine.
ecology_states.boundary: Project terrain description; not proof of malicious coordination.

ecology_states.description: Source lineage, context and corrections become easier to retrieve while historical versions remain inspectable.

concrete_mechanism_cases.observation: Crossmark lets publishers register corrections, retractions and other editorially significant updates as linked metadata, so a reader can discover that an older publication's status has changed without deleting the original record.
measurable_questions: Does the original record expose the update at retrieval time?
Does a downloaded PDF expose current status when Crossmark is embedded?
How long after the status change was update metadata registered?
concrete_mechanism_cases.why_it_matters: This is a practical model for making current status travel with durable historical records instead of relying on a searcher to independently discover a correction.

concrete_mechanism_cases.observation: MediaWiki stores sequential revisions with IDs, timestamps and metadata and exposes history/diff tools, allowing current content and earlier states to coexist as inspectable versions.
measurable_questions: Can a reader link to the exact historical version?
Can two versions be directly compared?
Which revisions are hidden from ordinary users and why?
concrete_mechanism_cases.why_it_matters: Versioned history makes later correction compatible with provenance: the current representation can change without making the earlier public state unrecoverable.

concrete_mechanism_cases.observation: Federated social objects can be delivered across independent servers and applications, creating derivative copies and conversational context across administrative boundaries.
measurable_questions: Which server is the provenance root?
What survives when one server removes or loses the source object?
Do replies and quotes preserve enough lineage to reconstruct context?
concrete_mechanism_cases.why_it_matters: Federation increases the importance of copy lineage: distributed availability can improve resilience while also making deletion, correction and context synchronization more complex.

concrete_mechanism_cases.observation: YouTube supports appeals and reports appeals/reinstatements for Community Guidelines enforcement, creating an observable status-change loop from sanction to re-review to possible reversal.
measurable_questions: Was the original sanction visible to an audience or only the creator?
Did reversal restore the same object/account state?
Can downstream references to the sanction discover the reversal?
Which sanction categories are excluded from the transparency metric being cited?
concrete_mechanism_cases.why_it_matters: A corrected platform decision is not automatically a corrected public memory; the ecological question is whether the changed status reaches the same retrieval and audience surfaces.

source_counting_rule: Count provenance roots, not visible repetitions. A hundred pages deriving from one root source are one corroboration root plus a distribution graph, not one hundred independent confirmations.
correction_ecology_rule: Measure correction as a propagation problem: authoring a correction, linking it to the original, distributing it, exposing it in search/archive surfaces and reducing recurrence are separate stages.
